- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- code-review: Review the current diff, or a PR number/branch/path target, for correctness bugs and reuse/simplification/efficiency cleanups at the given effort level (low/medium: fewer, high-confidence findings; high→max: broader coverage, may include uncertain findings; ultra: deep multi-agent review in the cloud (requires claude.ai account access)); with no level given, it reuses the level you typed last. Pass --comment to post findings as inline PR comments, or --fix to apply the findings to the working tree after the review. For ultra on a GitHub.com PR target, --post asks to post the finished review’s findings to the PR as a single comment from the user’s GitHub account (not a review; the launch dialog still confirms in interactive sessions, while non-interactive mode posts on the flag alone) and --no-post hides that option.
- simplify: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo). Omit the interval to let the model self-pace. - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- claude-api: Reference for the Claude API / Anthropic SDK — model ids, pricing, params, streaming, tool use, MCP, agents, caching, token counting, model migration.
TRIGGER — read BEFORE opening the target file; don't skip because it "looks like a one-liner" — whenever: the prompt names Claude/Anthropic in any form (Claude, Anthropic, Fable, Opus, Sonnet, Haiku, `anthropic`, `@anthropic-ai`, `claude-*`, `us.anthropic.*`, `[1m]`); the user asks about an LLM (pricing/model choice/limits/caching) — never answer from memory; OR the task is LLM-shaped with provider unstated (agent/MCP/tool-definition/multi-agent/RAG/LLM-judge/computer-use; generate/summarize/extract/classify/rewrite/converse over NL; debugging refusals/cutoffs/streaming/tool-calls/tokens).

- run: Launch and drive this project's app to see a change working. Use when asked to run, start, or screenshot the app, or to confirm a change works in the real app (not just tests). First looks for a project skill that already covers launching the app; otherwise falls back to built-in patterns per project type (CLI, server, TUI, Electron, browser-driven, library).

1	import { z } from "zod";
2	
3	/**
4	 * Defaults, declared once and referenced by both schemas below.
5	 *
6	 * `rainGuard` is ON because the protective behaviour already shipped inside
7	 * `weatherRules` — defaulting it off would silently change the generator for
8	 * every existing user. `tempUnit` is Celsius because every stored threshold,
9	 * and the text sent to the model, is Celsius; the unit is a display choice and
10	 * never reaches the rules.
11	 */
12	export const PREFERENCE_DEFAULTS = {
13	  rainGuard: true,
14	  tempUnit: "C",
15	  /** The local date the evening wear confirmation was last ANSWERED. */
16	  wearAskedOn: null,
17	} as const;
18	
19	/**
20	 * The STRICT schema — the write path.
21	 *
22	 * `PreferencesSchema.partial()` validates an incoming patch, and it must reject
23	 * a bad value rather than quietly repairing it: garbage accepted here is stored
24	 * forever and paid for on every later read.
25	 *
26	 * Only preferences something actually reads belong here. A stored flag that no
27	 * code consults is a switch that lies to the user.
28	 */
29	export const PreferencesSchema = z.object({
30	  rainGuard: z.boolean().default(PREFERENCE_DEFAULTS.rainGuard),
31	  tempUnit: z.enum(["C", "F"]).default(PREFERENCE_DEFAULTS.tempUnit),
32	  /**
33	   * Not a toggle — bookkeeping. Set by BOTH answers to the evening
34	   * confirmation, so the question is asked at most once a day whichever way it
35	   * went. Null means never answered.
36	   */
37	  wearAskedOn: z.string().nullable().default(PREFERENCE_DEFAULTS.wearAskedOn),
38	});
39	
40	export type Preferences = z.infer<typeof PreferencesSchema>;
41	
42	/**
43	 * The LENIENT mirror — the read path.
44	 *
45	 * `.catch()` sits on each field rather than on the object, so one malformed
46	 * value falls back on its own instead of discarding every other preference
47	 * alongside it. Defaults come from the same constant as the strict schema, and
48	 * `preferences.test.ts` asserts the two schemas keep identical keys, so adding
49	 * a preference to one and forgetting the other fails the suite.
50	 */
51	const LenientSchema = z.object({
52	  rainGuard: PreferencesSchema.shape.rainGuard.catch(PREFERENCE_DEFAULTS.rainGuard),
53	  tempUnit: PreferencesSchema.shape.tempUnit.catch(PREFERENCE_DEFAULTS.tempUnit),
54	  wearAskedOn: PreferencesSchema.shape.wearAskedOn.catch(PREFERENCE_DEFAULTS.wearAskedOn),
55	});
56	
57	/** Read the stored bag, repairing anything unreadable. */
58	export function readPreferences(raw: unknown): Preferences {
59	  const source = raw && typeof raw === "object" ? raw : {};
60	  return LenientSchema.parse(source);
61	}

-- The evening confirmation asks ONLY about looks the user actually opened, so
-- opening one has to leave a trace. Nothing recorded that before this.
--
-- Why it matters: the alternative — asking about today's drop — would offer a
-- "Yes" on a look the user never saw, and a Yes there is a fabricated wear.
-- wear_logs is the foundation of cost-per-wear, streaks, most-worn and gap
-- analysis, so a fabricated row poisons every one of them permanently, with no
-- way afterwards to tell it from a real one. That is exactly why the
-- "Auto-log worn looks" toggle was rejected twice.
--
-- A column on `outfits`, not a views table: the question is "was it opened, and
-- when most recently", never a history. One timestamp answers it.
alter table public.outfits
  add column if not exists viewed_at timestamptz;

-- The confirmation reads "today's outfits that were viewed, most recent first".
create index if not exists outfits_viewed_idx
  on public.outfits (user_id, generated_on, viewed_at desc)
  where viewed_at is not null;

Based on my review of all changed files and their context:

**What I checked:**
- `noteOutfitViewed` server action: authenticates via `supabase.auth.getUser()`, explicitly scopes the update by both `id` AND `user_id`, backed by RLS policy `outfits_own` (confirmed in `20260718090000_outfits.sql`). No SQL injection (parameterized), no injection into the timestamp value (server-generated).
- Client `useEffect` calls the server action with `outfit.id` — Next.js server actions have framework CSRF protection; even a spoofed `outfitId` from a compromised client can only affect the caller's own rows (double-scoped).
- Migration adds a nullable column with a partial index — no backfill/data-integrity concern, no lock-heavy operation on a hot table (nullable add is metadata-only in Postgres 11+).
- `shouldAsk` is a pure function with `===` comparison on strings; no injection sink.
- Preferences schema: `wearAskedOn` added consistently to defaults, strict schema, and lenient mirror (registry fanout — no missed consumer). The value is per-user own data written through `updatePreferences` which scopes by `user.id`.
- Sibling handlers (`toggleWear`, `toggleFavorite`) share the same auth pattern; parity holds. `toggleFavorite` predates this diff and omits explicit `user_id` in the update — pre-existing, not this diff.
- No new observability sinks (no logs/traces added); no dynamic loader; no shell/exec; no HTML rendering; no allowlist changes; no auth-gate changes; no IaC/CI changes.

**No security findings.**
